lesson.title: not: Flipping True and False
lesson.summary: The not operator takes a single boolean expression and inverts it, turning True into False and False into True, giving programs a way to express the opposite of a condition.
lesson.body:
Unlike and and or, which each combine two boolean expressions, not works on just one. It is placed directly before a boolean expression and produces the opposite value: if the expression it is applied to evaluates to True, not turns the whole thing into False, and if the expression evaluates to False, not turns it into True. This makes not the natural way to express ideas like "unless," "is not," or "does not," where a program cares about the absence of a condition rather than its presence.

Because not can be applied to any boolean expression, including one built from comparisons or from and and or, it can invert conditions of arbitrary complexity, not just simple variables. It is worth noting that not binds tightly to the single expression that follows it; when combined with and or or in a longer expression without parentheses, not is applied first, before the other operators are evaluated, as mentioned when logical operators were introduced.

Trace this example:

is_raining = False
stay_inside = not is_raining
print(stay_inside)

is_raining holds the boolean value False. not is_raining inverts that single value: since is_raining is False, not is_raining evaluates to True. stay_inside is bound to True, correctly representing the idea that it is not raining, so there is no reason to stay inside, as a direct True result rather than forcing the reader to reason through a double negative.

There is a well known pair of equivalences, sometimes called De Morgan's laws, that connect not to and and or: not (a and b) always produces the same result as (not a) or (not b), and not (a or b) always produces the same result as (not a) and (not b). Practically, this means "it is not the case that both conditions hold" is the same as "at least one of them fails," and "it is not the case that either condition holds" is the same as "both of them fail." These equivalences are genuinely useful for rewriting an awkward, heavily negated condition into a clearer one, and recognizing them will make some tricky boolean expressions much easier to reason about correctly.

Because not can be applied to any expression, not just ones that are already strictly boolean, it also participates in the truthiness rules explored later in this chapter: not [] evaluates to True, because an empty list is treated as equivalent to False, and inverting that gives True. Applying not twice, as in not not x, is occasionally used specifically to convert any value into a genuine boolean, since the first not inverts x according to truthiness and the second inverts it back, leaving a plain True or False rather than the original value untouched; the built-in bool() function, covered later in this chapter, is the clearer way to accomplish that same conversion.

Because not always produces a plain boolean result regardless of what kind of expression it was applied to, it can itself be combined with and or or to build a larger boolean expression, exactly like any comparison covered earlier in this chapter, and it can be nested as deeply as a piece of logic requires.
